title: Senior's toolkit: shipping and watching integrations
summary: Tag images by commit, promote by digest, roll out with a check, and read health, metrics and logs during a release.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: shipping and watching integrations
steps.body: Build once, promote the same image everywhere, and know within minutes whether a release hurt anyone. These are the commands behind that.

toolkit.what: Builds the image once and tags it with the commit it came from, so any running container can be traced back to its code.
flags: record the commit inside the image too
toolkit.example: docker buildx build -t ghcr.io/acme/orders:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD) --push .

toolkit.what: Reads an image's digest and copies an image between registries or repositories without pulling or rebuilding it. Promotion means copying the exact bytes you tested.
flags: copy all layers and platforms registry to registry

toolkit.what: Shows an image's digest and its platforms (amd64, arm64) from the registry, without pulling it.
Waits until a new version is fully rolled out and fails if it does not get there, so the pipeline stops instead of declaring success.
toolkit.example: kubectl rollout status deploy/orders -n integration --timeout=3m || kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders -n integration

toolkit.what: Live says the process works; ready says it can serve, with its dependencies reachable. Check both after a deploy and when traffic drops.
flags: a non-200 fails the step and shows which check failed
the one load balancers and Kubernetes use to send traffic

toolkit.what: Two queries that tell you whether a release hurt users: the share of 5xx responses, and the 95th percentile latency.
flags: per-second rate over the last 5 minutes
keep the bucket label for percentiles

toolkit.what: Reads the logs of every pod of a service at once, for the window you care about. With JSON logs, jq finds one trace id.
flags: show which pod each line came from

steps.prompt: Match each command to its part of a release.
pairs: fail the pipeline if the rollout stalls
check the new pods can serve

steps.prompt: Staging passed, but production behaves differently after the release. The pipeline ran `docker build -t orders:latest .` in the production job. What went wrong in the process?
options: Production got a fresh build, not the image that was tested; build once, then promote that digest
The health check is too strict
steps.explain: A rebuild can pick up a new base image, a new package version or different config. Tag by commit, test that image, and promote the same digest with `crane copy` (or a retag) so production runs exactly what staging ran.

steps.prompt: Roll out, and roll back automatically if the new version does not become ready in time.
steps.code: kubectl rollout __1__ deploy/orders -n integration --__2__=3m || kubectl rollout __3__ deploy/orders -n integration
steps.explain: `rollout status` exits non-zero when the timeout passes before all new pods are ready; `rollout undo` goes back to the previous revision.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes after a release, the dashboard shows the error ratio went from 0.2% to 4%, all `502` from the orders route. Pods are `Running` and `/health/live` is 200. What do you do first?
options: Roll back (`kubectl rollout undo`), then investigate with logs and the trace ids from the failing calls
Wait an hour to see if it settles
steps.explain: The release is the most likely cause and users are hurting now. Roll back first, which is cheap because the old image is still there, then find the cause. Live being 200 only says the process is up, not that it can reach its dependencies.

steps.prompt: Put a release of one image in order.
lines: Build and push the image tagged with the commit
Deploy it to staging and run the contract and smoke tests
Promote the same digest to the production registry
Deploy to production and wait with `kubectl rollout status`
Watch the error ratio and p95 for 15 minutes

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Never rebuild for production: promote the digest you tested. After every release, keep the error-ratio and p95 queries open for fifteen minutes, and decide in advance which numbers mean "roll back now".
